source.text: The City of Yuma is a Home Rule Municipality that is the most populous city in Yuma County, Colorado, United States. The population was 3,524 at the 2010 census.
source.title: Yuma, Colorado

source.text: The Yuma County Library District serves the population of Yuma County, Arizona. Today the library district consists of the nearly 80,000 square foot Main Library located in Yuma as well as branches in downtown Yuma, the Foothills, Somerton, San Luis, Wellton, Dateland, and Roll. The first Yuma Library, a Carnegie library, opened February 24, 1921 with 1,053 volumes and seating for 20 persons. Located in Sunset Park, the Yuma Carnegie Library underwent several expansions and renovations over the years, including a $4.2 million renovation completed in 2009. The Yuma Carnegie library still operates today as the Heritage Branch Library in downtown Yuma.
source.title: Yuma County Library District

source.text: Tucson is located 118 mi (190 km) southeast of Phoenix and 60 mi (97 km) north of the United States - Mexico border. The 2010 United States Census puts the city's population at 520,116 with a metropolitan area population at 980,263. In 2009, Tucson ranked as the 32nd largest city and 52nd largest metropolitan area in the United States. A major city in the Arizona Sun Corridor, Tucson is the largest city in southern Arizona, the second largest in the state after Phoenix. It is also the largest city in the area of the Gadsden Purchase. As of 2015, The Greater Tucson Metro area has exceeded a population of 1 million.
source.title: Tucson, Arizona

source.text: At the University of Arizona, where records have been kept since 1894, the record maximum temperature was 115 °F (46 °C) on June 19, 1960, and July 28, 1995, and the record minimum temperature was 6 °F (−14 °C) on January 7, 1913. There are an average of 150.1 days annually with highs of 90 °F (32 °C) or higher and an average of 26.4 days with lows reaching or below the freezing mark. Average annual precipitation is 11.15 in (283 mm). There is an average of 49 days with measurable precipitation. The wettest year was 1905 with 24.17 in (614 mm) and the driest year was 1924 with 5.07 in (129 mm). The most precipitation in one month was 7.56 in (192 mm) in July 1984. The most precipitation in 24 hours was 4.16 in (106 mm) on October 1, 1983. Annual snowfall averages 0.7 in (1.8 cm). The most snow in one year was 7.2 in (18 cm) in 1987. The most snow in one month was 6.0 in (15 cm) in January 1898 and March 1922.
source.title: Tucson, Arizona

Prompt version: musique-sparql-evidence-first-v1

ROLE

You are constructing the SPARQL computation for a multi-hop question-answering

Your job is to express a query whose ?answer value is obtained by executing
graph patterns against the RDF graph supplied below.

WHY THE QUERY STRUCTURE MATTERS

The query is executed over the frozen graph.

After execution, the computation is traced backwards to determine which RDF
statements contributed to each returned answer, and those RDF statements are
resolved back to their exact source occurrences.

Therefore the answer must genuinely arise from graph matching.

A query that simply injects an already-known answer may return the right value,
but it does not express the computation we need to observe.

THE FROZEN GRAPH IS THE SOURCE OF TRUTH FOR THIS TASK

Every triple pattern you rely on must correspond to relations actually available
in the frozen RDF graph.

Do not invent a relation because it would make the reasoning chain work.

Do not assume a benchmark relation exists unless you can locate the corresponding
RDF triple in the supplied graph.

If the graph does not contain the relation needed for an intended reasoning
step, do not fabricate it.

DECOMPOSITION

The MuSiQue decomposition describes the intended semantic dependency of the
question.

Use it to understand what each reasoning step means and to look for corresponding
relations in the frozen graph.

The decomposition does not create facts in the graph.

An intermediate answer from the decomposition may help you recognize entities,
but the SPARQL computation must still derive its bindings through the graph
relations that actually exist.

CONSTRUCT THE QUERY

Find the RDF triples in the frozen graph that can realize the question.

Use variables to connect dependent graph patterns.

The final ?answer variable must occur in an RDF triple pattern that retrieves
its value from the graph.

    <Organization> <abbreviatedAs> <FIFA> .

To retrieve the organization represented by FIFA:

    ?answer <abbreviatedAs> <FIFA> .

Do not instead write:

    <Organization> <abbreviatedAs> <FIFA> .
    BIND(<Organization> AS ?answer)

The first query derives the answer.
The second query inserts an answer that was already known.

SUPPORTED QUERY FORM

Use a SELECT query with ?answer as the answer variable.

Use basic RDF triple patterns and joins through shared variables.

Do not use:
- BIND
- VALUES
- SELECT DISTINCT
- GRAPH
- SERVICE
- SPARQL updates
- FROM clauses

Python adds dataset scoping after your semantic query is produced.

MATCHED TRIPLES

on while constructing the query.

Do not report a triple that is not present in the graph.

matched_triples describes your evidence selection; the SPARQL query describes
